content: Dental fluorosis is a condition that arises due to excessive fluoride intake, which can occur through natural fluoride in water, water fluoridation, toothpaste, or other sources. The damage to tooth development typically happens between the ages of 6 months and 5 years, during the period when teeth are forming. Teeth are primarily composed of hydroxyapatite and carbonated hydroxyapatite, but in the presence of fluoride, fluorapatite is formed. These changes can make the teeth appear aesthetically unpleasing. Importantly, dental fluorosis cannot develop after the teeth have erupted into the oral cavity. In mild cases of dental fluorosis, the enamel may exhibit small white flecks or pits. In more severe cases, brown stains may appear on the teeth. Although permanent teeth are more commonly affected, primary teeth can occasionally show signs of fluorosis. Differential diagnoses for dental fluorosis include Turner's hypoplasia (which is usually localized), mild forms of amelogenesis imperfecta, and other environmental enamel defects that present as diffuse or demarcated opacities. H.T. Dean's fluorosis index, developed in 1942, remains the most widely accepted classification system for dental fluorosis. This index assigns a fluorosis score based on the most severe form of fluorosis observed on at least two teeth. The prevalence of dental fluorosis has been studied in the United States through surveys conducted by the National Institute of Dental Research (1986–1987) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (1999–2002). These studies revealed a 9% increase in the prevalence of dental fluorosis among American children over a 20-year period. Additionally, African American children were found to have higher rates of fluorosis compared to Caucasian children. The condition is more common in rural areas where drinking water is sourced from shallow wells or hand pumps, particularly when the fluoride concentration in the water exceeds 1 part per million (ppm). Children with poor calcium intake are also at greater risk. To consume 1 mg of fluoride from water fluoridated at 1 ppm, an individual would need to drink one liter of water. It is unlikely for a person to exceed the tolerable upper limit of fluoride intake from optimally fluoridated water alone. However, excessive fluoride consumption can occur when fluoridated water is combined with other sources, such as swallowing fluoridated toothpaste, consuming fluoride-rich foods, or taking fluoride supplements. The use of fluoride supplements to prevent tooth decay has become rare in areas with water fluoridation, though it was commonly recommended by dentists in the UK until the early 1990s. Preventing dental fluorosis involves reducing fluoride intake to levels below the tolerable upper limit. Treatment for dental fluorosis is primarily cosmetic and is performed by a dentist. The cost and success of treatment vary depending on the severity of the condition and the chosen method. Common treatment options include tooth bleaching, microabrasion, and conservative composite restorations or porcelain veneers. Bleaching and microabrasion are typically used for superficial stains, while conservative restorations are employed for more severe aesthetic concerns.
